why: A grain haulier with 1,150 to 1,620 farm customers paying about $1,000 a month, silos handling 2,900 to 5,300 tons a week at $6 to $9 a ton, and thin haulage margins beside fatter silo margins is believable.
All four rating pies add to 100%, and survey samples of 780 and 1,140 customers per delivery zone are plausible for an online grocer.
A 24-hour club selling day passes to 22,000 different people a year, with 63% coming once, works out to a few dozen one-off visitors a day, which is believable for a large club.

An online grocer growing from $18 million to $116 million in revenue while its losses shrink from -153% to -27% of revenue implies costs of about $45 million to $147 million, a believable cash-burning delivery start-up.

Furniture zones with $15 million to $44 million in sales and advertising budgets of $1.2 million to $4.2 million (roughly 4% to 14% of sales) are believable, if a little advertising-heavy in some zones.
About 1.2 million students, commuters and retirees in a regional bus operator's area, with most contacted residents in cities, is believable.
Wholesale and café profits add to the stated totals each year (40, 40, 30, 20), and margins of 8% to 4% imply steady sales of about $500 million, which is believable for a coffee roaster with cafés.
A water-cooler van costing $560 a day with its driver, offices paying $35 a week for six 19-litre bottles, and a break-even route of about 80 offices (around 34 stops a day) is believable.
Every score distribution adds to 100% for both groups, and a mobile network surveying 54,000 people before a launch is plausible.
Household incomes converting to about $9,500 to $61,000 at basic exchange rates are believable for four foreign markets, and the PPP figures stay within a few times realistic levels.
